title: BITOXIN: Preserving State Dependencies to Expose Integrity Failures in Stateful Quality Assurance
abstract: State corruption may escape quality assurance when tests discard live state before checking it, reuse an unchecked result as their expectation, or observe only values that no longer depend on the corrupted state. This paper presents BITOXIN as a test-design method that combines persistent state, dependent operations, permitted execution interruptions, and independently specified observations. The method draws on established stateful-testing and fault-observability ideas; its reference implementation is a resumable integrity probe, not a prerequisite for product adoption. We specify its detection assumptions and evaluate observation policies through 61,440 enumerated single-bit-injection trials and 120 clean controls. For faults inserted at five bit-walk boundaries, retaining state and performing a final scan detects all 15,360 faults assigned to that policy. Omitting the scan detects 7,680; reconstructing clean state detects none. A further 15,360 trials show that corruption behind an advancing verifier can escape the current pass but is detected in the next retained pass under the stated model. Native ARM64, portable-C, and sanitizer configurations produce identical outcome records. These results validate a narrow observation mechanism rather than establish field defect coverage or improved time to discovery. We also describe how to transfer the method to protected-value libraries and transaction services without deploying a Linux module.
